hint: A specific chip, chip family or CPU core. Microcontrollers and console CPUs count; bare instruction sets like x86 do not.

answers.l: Intel launched the original Pentium in 1993. Its FDIV division bug, found by Thomas Nicely in 1994, led Intel to take a $475 million charge.
Launched in 1975 at $25, far below rivals. Versions of it powered the Apple II, Commodore 64, Atari 2600 and NES.
Released by Federico Faggin's Zilog in 1976. It ran 8080 code and powered the TRS-80, ZX Spectrum and countless CP/M machines.
Apple's first Mac system on a chip, announced in November 2020, built on TSMC's 5 nm process with 16 billion transistors.
Released in 1971 for a Busicom calculator. It is widely called the first commercial single-chip microprocessor, with about 2,300 transistors.
Intel's 1974 8-bit chip powered the Altair 8800, and Gary Kildall's CP/M operating system was written for it.
Introduced in 1978, its 16-bit instruction set gave the x86 family its name.
An 8086 with an 8-bit external data bus. IBM chose it for the original IBM PC in 1981 so it could use cheaper support chips.
Intel's first 32-bit x86 chip, from 1985. Linus Torvalds wrote the first Linux kernel in 1991 on his new 386 PC.
Launched in 1989, the first x86 chip with over a million transistors. The DX version put the floating-point unit on the chip.
Motorola's 1979 chip powered the original Macintosh, the Amiga, the Atari ST and the Sega Genesis.
The Core i7 brand debuted in November 2008 with Nehalem desktop chips, which moved the memory controller onto the processor die.
Intel launched the first Core i5, the Lynnfield-based i5-750, in September 2009.
AMD's Ryzen line launched in March 2017 on the Zen microarchitecture and made AMD competitive again on the desktop.
Intel and HP's 64-bit IA-64 chip shipped in 2001, earned the nickname Itanic, and made its final shipments in 2021.
Intel's budget brand began in 1998. The first Celeron, codenamed Covington, had no L2 cache at all.
Intel's server and workstation brand since 1998, starting with the Pentium II Xeon.
Launched in 2000 on NetBurst, whose long pipeline chased clock speed. Intel cancelled the planned 4 GHz version in 2004.
AMD's 1999 Athlon became the first x86 processor to reach 1 GHz, announced in March 2000 just ahead of Intel.
Released in 2006 on the Core microarchitecture, it replaced NetBurst and put Intel back in the performance lead.
Apple's second-generation Mac chip, announced at WWDC in June 2022 and first shipped in the MacBook Air and 13-inch MacBook Pro.
Motorola's 1974 8-bit chip. Several of its designers, including Chuck Peddle, left for MOS and created the cheaper 6502.
AMD's server processor line launched in June 2017 on Zen, combining multiple dies in one package.
Introduced in the iPhone 5s in September 2013 as the first 64-bit processor in a smartphone.
Announced in October 2023, the first Apple Mac chips built on a 3 nm process.
Debuted in the iPad Pro in May 2024 before reaching Macs later that year.
Intel's 1995 Pentium Pro debuted the P6 design, which decoded x86 into micro-ops and executed them out of order.
Released in 1997 in a Slot 1 cartridge rather than a socket, with its L2 cache chips mounted on the cartridge board.
Launched in 1999 with SSE instructions. Its per-chip serial number drew privacy protests and was dropped from later models.
Intel's 1982 chip added protected mode and powered IBM's PC/AT in 1984.
Intel's first 8-bit processor, from 1972, was designed for Datapoint's 2200 terminal, which ended up not using it.
Intel's 1976 successor to the 8080 needed only a single 5-volt power supply.
Intel introduced the Core i9 brand in 2017 with high-end Skylake-X desktop processors.
Core i3 arrived in January 2010 with Clarkdale chips, which put a separate graphics die in the same package as the CPU.
AMD's 2003 desktop chip brought 64-bit x86 to consumer PCs. Intel later adopted AMD's 64-bit extensions.
Released in April 2003, it was the first processor to implement AMD64, the 64-bit extension of x86.
The PowerPC 750, marketed by Apple as the G3, powered the original iMac in 1998.
Motorola's PowerPC 7400 added AltiVec vector instructions. Apple advertised the 1999 Power Mac G4 as a supercomputer.
IBM's PowerPC 970 shipped in the Power Mac G5 in 2003. Difficulty fitting it into laptops helped push Apple to Intel.
The PlayStation 2's CPU, designed by Sony and Toshiba around a MIPS core with two vector units.
Qualcomm's line of mobile systems on a chip, announced in 2007 and used in many Android flagship phones.
Designed by Sony, Toshiba and IBM for the PlayStation 3, pairing one PowerPC core with eight SPE vector units, one disabled in the PS3.
Intel's low-power x86 line launched in 2008 and ran most netbooks of that era.
Apple's first in-house system on a chip, introduced with the original iPad in 2010 and also used in the iPhone 4.
A 2003 mobile chip from Intel's Haifa team, based on P6 rather than NetBurst. Its design led directly to the Core line.
A 1997 Pentium revision that added the 57 MMX integer SIMD instructions.
Intel's first dual-core desktop processor, released in 2005 and built from two NetBurst cores.
Intel Core Duo powered the first Intel Macs, the iMac and MacBook Pro, in January 2006.
Released in 1982 with timers and DMA built in, it was mostly used in embedded systems rather than PCs.
Intel's brand since late 2023, starting with Meteor Lake chips assembled from separate tiles with Foveros packaging.
Intel's many-core x86 line grew out of the Larrabee GPU project and was discontinued around 2020.
AMD's 386 clone shipped in 1991 after a legal fight with Intel and sold in large numbers.
AMD's first fully in-house x86 design, released in 1996, translated x86 instructions into RISC-like operations.
Released in 1997, it was based on the Nx686 design AMD gained by acquiring NexGen.
Introduced in 1998 with 3DNow!, AMD's own SIMD instructions for floating-point math.
AMD's budget Athlon variant, launched in 2000 to compete with Intel's Celeron.
AMD's budget brand from 2004, replacing Duron.
AMD's first quad-core desktop chip of 2007. A TLB bug in early steppings forced a workaround that cut performance.
Bulldozer-based FX chips were sold as eight-core. AMD paid $12.1 million in 2019 to settle a lawsuit over that claim.
AMD's high-end desktop line launched in 2017 with up to 16 cores, later reaching 64.
Motorola's 1978 8-bit chip with 16-bit features, used in the TRS-80 Color Computer and the Vectrex console.
Motorola's fully 32-bit 68k chip of 1984, used in the Macintosh II.
Added an on-chip memory management unit and powered the original NeXT Computer and the Macintosh SE/30.
Motorola's 1990 chip integrated the floating-point unit and ran the NeXTstation and Macintosh Quadra.
The first PowerPC chip from the Apple, IBM and Motorola alliance, shipped in the first Power Macintosh in 1994.
IBM's three-core PowerPC CPU for the Xbox 360, released in 2005.
The NES CPU: a 6502 core with decimal mode removed and an audio unit added.
A 6502 variant with a built-in I/O port, used as the CPU of the Commodore 64.
A CMOS version of the 6502 with added instructions, still produced by Western Design Center.
A 16-bit extension of the 6502 by Western Design Center. It powered the Apple IIGS, and a Ricoh variant ran the SNES.
DEC's first Alpha chip, launched in 1992, a 64-bit RISC design that led its era in clock speed.
DEC's fast, low-power ARM design from 1996 ran the Newton MessagePad 2000. Intel took over the line in 1998 and later made XScale.
Sun's first 64-bit SPARC chip of 1995, which introduced the VIS multimedia instructions.
MIPS's 1988 chip. A variant served as the CPU of the original Sony PlayStation.
Transmeta's 2000 chip ran x86 code through code-morphing software on a VLIW core. Linus Torvalds worked at Transmeta.
The first ARM chip, designed at Acorn by Sophie Wilson and Steve Furber and first run in 1985. It once ran with its power supply disconnected, fed by leakage current.
A 1990s ARM core with Thumb instructions that ran the Game Boy Advance and early iPods.
Raspberry Pi's first in-house microcontroller, released in 2021 on the Raspberry Pi Pico.
Espressif's cheap Wi-Fi microcontroller caught hobbyists' attention in 2014 when modules sold for a few dollars.
STMicroelectronics' family of ARM Cortex-M microcontrollers, launched in 2007.
NVIDIA's mobile chip line. The Tegra X1 powers the original Nintendo Switch.
Samsung's system-on-chip line, used in many Galaxy phones.
Google's first in-house phone chip, debuting in the Pixel 6 in 2021.
Amazon's ARM server CPU, designed by its Annapurna Labs unit and first offered on EC2 in 2018.
Qualcomm's chip that brought its Nuvia-derived Oryon cores to Windows laptops in 2024.
Intel's 1981 32-bit design with hardware support for objects and capabilities. It was slow and a commercial failure.
Intel's 1989 RISC chip was hard to program efficiently but was used in the Intel Paragon supercomputer.
Intel's 1988 embedded RISC chip, widely used in laser printers, RAID controllers and military systems.
Intel's MCS-48 microcontroller from 1976. An 8048 served as the CPU of the Magnavox Odyssey 2 console.
Intel's 1974 successor to the 4004, adding interrupts and more instructions.
A 1988 cost-reduced 386 with a 16-bit external data bus, letting PC makers build cheaper boards.
The 1991 486SX had its floating-point unit disabled or absent. The 487SX coprocessor was essentially a full 486DX.
AMD's 486-compatible chips of 1993 stayed popular as cheap upgrades well into the Pentium era.
A low-power x86 line AMD acquired from National Semiconductor. The Geode LX powered the OLPC XO-1 laptop.
AMD's 32-bit RISC chip from 1987, widely used in laser printers and other embedded systems.
The last of the 68k line, from 1994. It saw little desktop use but was popular in Amiga accelerator cards.
Motorola's 1988 RISC family sold poorly, and Motorola then joined Apple and IBM to build PowerPC.
Motorola's 8-bit microcontroller of the mid-1980s, a staple of robotics projects and university courses.
IBM's 2001 POWER4 was the first commercial microprocessor with two cores on one die.
IBM's 2017 chip powered Summit and Sierra, two of the fastest US supercomputers of their time.
IBM's PowerPC 750 derivative clocked at 486 MHz, the CPU of the Nintendo GameCube.
The Wii's 729 MHz IBM PowerPC CPU, a faster evolution of the GameCube's Gekko.
The Super Nintendo's CPU, a Ricoh chip built around a 65C816 core.
A cheaper 6502 with only 13 address lines, limiting it to 8 KB of address space. It ran the Atari 2600.
The Game Boy's CPU, a Sharp chip whose SM83 core mixes features of the 8080 and the Z80.
Zilog's 1979 16-bit chip was not compatible with the Z80 and lost the market to Intel and Motorola.
Zilog's pipelined Z80 successor. It runs the TI-84 Plus CE graphing calculator.
RCA's 1976 CMOS COSMAC chip. Radiation-hardened versions flew on spacecraft including the Galileo probe to Jupiter.
One of the first single-chip 16-bit microprocessors, from 1976. It ran the TI-99/4A home computer.
Texas Instruments' 4-bit TMS1000 of 1974 is often cited as the first commercially available microcontroller.
DEC's 1998 Alpha EV6. AMD licensed its EV6 bus for the original Athlon.
Intel's ARM line derived from StrongARM. Its PXA chips ran many Pocket PCs before Intel sold the business to Marvell in 2006.
Sun's 2005 Niagara chip ran eight cores with four threads each, aiming at throughput over single-thread speed.
Fujitsu's chip that powered the K computer, ranked the world's fastest supercomputer in 2011.
Fujitsu's ARM chip with SVE vector extensions, powering Fugaku, the world's fastest supercomputer in 2020.
MIPS Computer Systems' first chip, released in 1986 and based on John Hennessy's Stanford MIPS research.
MIPS's 1991 chip was among the first 64-bit microprocessors.
NEC's MIPS chip derived from the R4300i, clocked at 93.75 MHz in the Nintendo 64.
MIPS's 1996 out-of-order chip powered SGI machines such as the Origin 2000 and Octane.
Hitachi's 32-bit SuperH chip. The Sega Saturn used two of them, and the 32X add-on another two.
A 200 MHz Hitachi SuperH chip served as the Sega Dreamcast's CPU.
Cyrix's 1996 x86 chip was sold with a PR rating that compared it to higher-clocked Pentiums.
VIA's low-power x86 chip from its Centaur design team, released in 2001.
Inmos's 1980s chip had built-in serial links for wiring many processors together and was programmed in occam.
Acorn's first production ARM chip, which ran the Archimedes from 1987. It had no cache.
ARM's first ARMv7-A application core. A Samsung chip using it ran the iPhone 3GS in 2009.
ARM's smallest Cortex-M core when announced in 2009. The RP2040 uses two of its M0+ successors.
ARM's 64-bit efficiency core announced in 2012, used in the Raspberry Pi 3 and huge numbers of phones.
Microchip's PIC16F84, with flash program memory, was a staple of 1990s hobbyist electronics projects.
Texas Instruments' 16-bit ultra-low-power microcontroller family, common in battery-powered sensors.
Ampere Computing's ARM server chip of 2020 offered up to 80 cores.
A Chinese CPU line from the Institute of Computing Technology, first MIPS-compatible and later using its own LoongArch ISA.
NEC's 1984 pin-compatible 8088 replacement ran faster and could also execute 8080 code.
IBM's mainframe chip announced in 2021 for the z16, with an on-chip accelerator for AI inference.
The Wii U's three-core IBM PowerPC CPU, an evolution of the Wii's Broadway.
Hudson Soft's 65C02-based CPU in the PC Engine, sold as the TurboGrafx-16 in North America.
Fairchild's 1975 8-bit processor, spread across multiple chips, ran the Fairchild Channel F console.
Signetics' 1975 8-bit chip, used in consoles such as the Emerson Arcadia 2001.
National Semiconductor's SC/MP, pronounced scamp, was a low-cost 8-bit chip from 1976.
The NS32016 of 1982 was among the first chips with a 32-bit architecture, but bugs and delays limited its success.
General Instrument's 16-bit chip that served as the CPU of Mattel's Intellivision.
A 1975 single-chip implementation of DEC's PDP-8 instruction set, used in DEC's VT78 and the original DECmate.
The MIPS-based CPU in Sony's PlayStation Portable, which launched in Japan in 2004.
Transmeta's 2004 second-generation chip, which ran x86 code by translating it in software onto a VLIW core.
Cyrix's 1990s chip combined an x86 core with graphics, audio and memory control for cheap PCs.
NexGen's 1994 x86 chip translated instructions into RISC-like operations. AMD bought NexGen in 1996.
IDT's Centaur-designed x86 chip of 1997, a simple, low-cost Pentium alternative. Centaur later went to VIA.
VIA's 64-bit out-of-order x86 design from 2008, built by its Centaur subsidiary.
AT&T's Hobbit was designed to run C code efficiently, powered the EO Personal Communicator, and was considered for Apple's Newton.
Fairchild's 1986 32-bit RISC-like chip, later taken over by Intergraph for its workstations.
HP's 1996 PA-RISC chip, its first 64-bit design, with out-of-order execution.
Elbrus processors from Russia's MCST use a VLIW design and can run x86 code through binary translation.
The 260-core Chinese chip inside Sunway TaihuLight, the world's fastest supercomputer from 2016 to 2018.
SiFive's 2018 Freedom U540 was marketed as the first Linux-capable multicore RISC-V processor.
Hitachi's CMOS 6809 clone has an undocumented native mode that adds registers and instructions.
A cut-down 68000 with an 8-bit data bus, used in the Sinclair QL.
Motorola's embedded chip family from the mid-1990s with a simplified 68k instruction set.
The RTX2010 executes Forth directly in hardware. Radiation-hardened versions flew on spacecraft such as the Philae comet lander.
AMD's Am9080 began in 1975 as an unlicensed reverse-engineered copy of Intel's 8080. Intel later licensed it.
A Soviet clone of the Intel 8080 used in many Eastern Bloc home computers.

nope.x86: An instruction set architecture, not a specific chip. Try the 8086 or 80386.
nope.ARM: A company and an instruction set. Name a chip or core, like the ARM7TDMI or Cortex-A53.
nope.RISC-V: An open instruction set, not a processor. A chip like the SiFive Freedom U540 counts.
nope.RTX 4090: A graphics card GPU, not a general-purpose CPU.
nope.Intel 8087: A floating-point coprocessor that needed an 8086 or 8088 to run programs; it was not a CPU on its own.
nope.TPU: Google's Tensor Processing Unit is a machine learning accelerator, not a general-purpose CPU.

traps.q: Which processor was in the new PC that Linus Torvalds was exploring when he started writing Linux in 1991?
traps.l: Torvalds wanted to learn the 386's protected mode and task switching, and the early Linux kernel was written specifically for that chip.

traps.q: Which 8-bit chip, sold for $25 at its 1975 launch when rivals cost far more, became the CPU of the Apple II?
traps.l: Chuck Peddle's team left Motorola to build it at MOS Technology, and its low price helped launch the home computer era.
